subject: Medicine
topic: Rabies Post-Exposure Prophylaxis HRIG and Inactivated Vaccine Schedule
stem: A 32-year-old man presents to the emergency department after waking up in his rustic mountain cabin in rural Pennsylvania to find a live bat flying around his bedroom. He does not recall being bitten or scratched, but states the bat landed near his pillow before flying away out an open window. The bat escaped and was not captured or tested. On examination, he is alert and oriented with normal vital signs. Thorough examination of his skin and scalp reveals no visible puncture wounds, abrasions, or bites. He has never received a rabies vaccine. Which of the following represents the most appropriate management regarding rabies post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP)?

options.text: Administration of the 4-dose rabies vaccine series alone, withholding HRIG because no bite wound is visible
options.explanation: Withholding HRIG in an unvaccinated patient leaves the patient completely unprotected against early viral neural migration before vaccine antibodies develop, resulting in fatal rabies.

options.text: Observation without prophylaxis, instructing the patient to return only if fever or agitation develops
options.explanation: Waiting for clinical symptoms (fever, hydrophobia, aerophobia) is universally fatal; rabies has near-100% mortality once symptoms appear.

options.text: Administration of human rabies immune globulin (HRIG) alone as a single injection without any vaccine series
options.explanation: HRIG provides transient passive protection lasting only 2 to 3 weeks; without active vaccine immunization, late rabies encephalitis will develop.

options.text: Immediate wound cleansing, full-dose human rabies immune globulin (HRIG) infiltrated around potential sites and IM, plus a 4-dose rabies vaccine series on days 0, 3, 7, and 14
options.explanation: This patient has an indication for RABIES POST-EXPOSURE PROPHYLAXIS (PEP) following a BAT EXPOSURE. Rabies is a lethal rhabdovirus (lyssavirus) that causes fatal acute progressive encephalomyelitis with a case-fatality rate approaching 100% once clinical symptoms appear. Bats are the primary reservoir for rabies in the United States (>70% of human cases). Because bat teeth are tiny and needle-sharp, bat bites can be COMPLETELY INVISIBLE AND UNNOTICED. CDC and ACIP guidelines strictly mandate: ANY PHYSICAL CONTACT OR UNWITNESSED DIRECT CONTACT WITH A BAT (e.g., finding a bat in a room with a sleeping person, an unattended child, or an intoxicated individual) IS CLASSIFIED AS A HIGH-RISK EXPOSURE REQUIRING IMMEDIATE RABIES PEP, UNLESS THE BAT IS CAPTURED AND TESTS NEGATIVE FOR RABIES. In a PREVIOUSLY UNVACCINATED INDIVIDUAL, PEP consists of two mandatory components initiated on Day 0: (1) PASSIVE IMMUNIZATION: HUMAN RABIES IMMUNE GLOBULIN (HRIG, 20 IU/kg). The full calculated dose should be infiltrated into and around any bite wounds; any remaining volume is injected intramuscularly at a site distant from vaccine administration (e.g., gluteus or vastus lateralis). HRIG provides immediate, life-saving neutralizing antibodies during the 7-10 days before active immune response; and (2) ACTIVE IMMUNIZATION: HUMAN DIPLOID CELL VACCINE (HDCV) OR PURIFIED CHICK EMBRYO CELL VACCINE (PCECV): A 4-DOSE SERIES ADMINISTERED INTRAMUSCULARLY IN THE DELTOID ON DAYS 0, 3, 7, AND 14 (a 5th dose on day 28 is added ONLY for immunocompromised patients). HRIG is never given after day 7 because active antibodies have already developed.

options.text: Topical povidone-iodine application to the head and scalp with a single booster vaccine dose
options.explanation: A single booster dose is indicated ONLY for PREVIOUSLY VACCINATED individuals (who receive vaccine on days 0 and 3 without HRIG); unvaccinated individuals require HRIG plus a 4-dose series.

subject: Medicine
topic: Streptococcal Toxic Shock Syndrome Clindamycin Protein Synthesis Suppression
stem: A 36-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with high fevers, confusion, and excruciating pain in her right thigh that developed 12 hours after a minor contusion sustained during softball. On arrival, she is in profound shock. Vital signs: temperature 39.8 C (103.6 F), blood pressure 72/40 mm Hg despite 3 liters of crystalloids, heart rate 138/min, and respiratory rate 28/min. Physical examination reveals an erythematous, exquisitely tender, swollen right thigh with a diffuse, blanching scarlatiniform macular erythroderma across her torso and limbs, with strawberry tongue. Emergency surgical exploration reveals intact fascia with edema and localized myositis; intraoperative Gram stain reveals Gram-positive cocci in chains, and blood cultures grow Group A Streptococcus (Streptococcus pyogenes). She is diagnosed with STREPTOCOCCAL TOXIC SHOCK SYNDROME (STSS) and necrotizing myositis. Antimicrobial therapy is initiated with high-dose intravenous aqueous penicillin G. Which of the following antimicrobial agents must be added immediately to penicillin to suppress bacterial exotoxin production and reduce mortality?

options.text: Intravenous gentamicin 5 mg/kg daily for synergistic cell wall penetration
options.explanation: Aminoglycosides are used for enterococcal and staphylococcal synergy; they do not suppress streptococcal exotoxin production and cause acute tubular necrosis.

options.text: Intravenous vancomycin monotherapy replacing penicillin G
options.explanation: Vancomycin targets cell wall synthesis and is also subject to the Eagle effect; it does not inhibit ribosomal protein synthesis or suppress superantigen exotoxin release.

options.text: Oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily as adjunctive antiribosomal therapy
options.explanation: Oral tetracyclines cannot achieve rapid bactericidal and antitoxin concentrations in vasoplegic septic shock; high-dose IV clindamycin is the proven standard.

options.text: Intravenous ciprofloxacin 400 mg every 12 hours for DNA gyrase inhibition
options.explanation: Fluoroquinolones inhibit DNA gyrase and do not shut down exotoxin translation; clindamycin is the guideline-directed antitoxin agent.

options.text: Intravenous clindamycin 900 mg every 8 hours
options.explanation: This patient has STREPTOCOCCAL TOXIC SHOCK SYNDROME (STSS) and necrotizing myositis caused by Group A Streptococcus (GAS, Streptococcus pyogenes). Pathogenesis is driven by BACTERIAL SUPERANTIGENS (specifically Streptococcal Pyrogenic Exotoxins A, B, and C [SPE-A/B/C]), which bypass normal antigen processing by cross-linking the variable beta-chain of the T-cell receptor (TCR V-beta) directly to MHC Class II molecules on antigen-presenting cells. This triggers uncontrolled, polyclonal activation of up to 20% of all circulating T cells, causing a massive systemic cytokine storm (TNF-alpha, IL-1, IL-6, IFN-gamma), capillary leak, refractory vasoplegic shock, and multi-organ failure. In high-inoculum, stationary-phase deep tissue infections, penicillin suffers from the 'EAGLE EFFECT' (loss of bactericidal efficacy because penicillin acts on penicillin-binding proteins that are downregulated when bacteria are stationary rather than actively dividing). The mandatory standard of care is the ADDITION OF INTRAVENOUS CLINDAMYCIN (600-900 mg IV every 8 hours) TO HIGH-DOSE PENICILLIN (or ampicillin). Clindamycin is a lincosamide that binds to the 50S RIBOSOMAL SUBUNIT, SHUTTING DOWN BACTERIAL PROTEIN SYNTHESIS. This: (1) Directly halts the transcription and translation of toxic pyrogenic exotoxins and M-protein; (2) Is unaffected by the Eagle effect or bacterial inoculum size; and (3) Enhances phagocytosis of streptococci. Observational and clinical studies demonstrate that adding clindamycin to beta-lactams significantly reduces mortality in STSS (from >40% down to <15-20%). Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) may be added to neutralize circulating superantigens.
